sentences.text: Vallibonavenatrix was a moderately sized bipedal predator belonging to the spinosaurid family.
Its back featured moderately tall neural spines, with one expanded into a trapezoidal, fan-like shape that researchers suggest formed a sail.
The skeleton shows deep depressions and air-filled pneumatic openings in the sacrum and ilium, indicating a highly pneumatic structure.
This specimen represents the most complete spinosaurid fossil ever found on the Iberian Peninsula.
Elisabete Malafaia and colleagues formally described the species Vallibonavenatrix cani in 2019 based on a partial skeleton.
The remains were found in the Arcillas de Morella Formation in Castellón, Spain, and include a cervical vertebra, six dorsal vertebrae, an almost complete sacrum, and fragments of ribs and chevrons.
The generic name Vallibonavenatrix combines the town of Vallibona with the Latin word for huntress, while the specific name 'cani' honors Juan Cano Forner.
Researchers suggest that the morphology of Vallibonavenatrix's neural spines may have formed a sail on its back.
In 2019, Malafaia and colleagues classified Vallibonavenatrix within the family Spinosauridae, a group of large-bodied tetanuran dinosaurs.
The team found the animal more closely related to spinosaurines like Spinosaurus than to baryonychines like Baryonyx, placing it in the subfamily Spinosaurinae.
Certain anatomical characteristics suggest Vallibonavenatrix may have an affinity with spinosaurines rather than baryonychines.
Vallibonavenatrix lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, between 129.4 and 125 million years ago.
It shared its environment with Iguanodon bernissartensis, Morelladon beltrani, an indeterminate sauropod, and the spinosaurid Protathlitis.

A 2021 study by Chris Barker and colleagues found Vallibonavenatrix's phylogenetic position unstable, placing it either as the most basal spinosaurid outside both subfamilies or within Baryonychinae depending on the analysis method.
A study by Octávio Mateus and Darío Estraviz-López in 2022 also did not find Vallibonavenatrix to be a spinosaurid.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Vallibonavenatrix as Baryonychinae.
However, a 2025 reassessment by Rauhut and colleagues recovered Vallibonavenatrix within Spinosaurinae, diverging after Iberospinus.
